codex.worst_flaw: The post-reward success rule uses digital completion alone, so the pilot can declare success without verifying that technicians still complete substantive checks before starting work.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no versioned event history, no shadow validation of how credit is counted, and no plan for how many crews the staggered comparison needs or how much uncertainty to expect, so it cannot reliably show whether the meal adds anything beyond the workflow fixes.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, fixing workflow barriers, protected stop-work rights, a credit rule that doesn't punish hazard holds, and a randomized stepped rollout with a post-reward check are strong, but a small meal reward is weak for a 35% baseline, and the default-first-screen change carries most of the durable effect.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: approved paper checks still lower a crew’s reward rate even when the outage window is extended, creating peer pressure to avoid the designated safe fallback.

claude.worst_flaw: A crew-level 70% meal threshold invites peer pressure and rushed or backfilled checklists. The design never adjusts goals for crew baselines, small job counts or case mix, and an 8-job weekly spot-check sample is too small to reliably detect gaming across 300 technicians.

holistic.reason: A carefully designed, union-co-developed pilot with fair counting rules, safeguards against gaming and pressure, and a built-in default and decision rule, though the crew-meal reward is modest, the measurement and spot-check setup is somewhat complex, and the 70% team threshold may feel remote to some crews.

claude.worst_flaw: Credit and the 10-job weekly audit rest on the app's own timestamps and on self-reported start or stop logs. There is no independent check of whether work actually started before the checklist, so backdated or rushed checklists could still earn credit, and the event history cannot be replayed or validated in shadow.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The shared payout counts approved paper checklists as misses, creating peer pressure to avoid the safe fallback when the app fails.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a fixed-up workflow, a fair counting rule, safeguards against rushed or pressured checks, and a staggered comparison make it approvable, but a one-hour release reward is small and hard to notice, and lasting change depends on whether the workflow fixes stick once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The shared all-or-nothing half-day reward for hitting 80% gives the whole group a reason to pressure colleagues or rush approvals near the threshold, and its value over the queue fixes alone is only tested weakly, with no protection for small-group inference and no staffed appeal or event-versioned audit beyond one coordinator.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot checks quality only for on-time decisions during reward weeks, so it can declare lasting success from faster reviews without knowing whether review quality deteriorated.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, using shared rather than individual rewards, and adding a quality check and a clear post-reward decision rule suit a sceptical team and guard against rushed reviews. The rules are complicated, the reward is a one-off half-day, and a six-week pilot may not lock in the habit, so durability is only moderate.

codex.worst_flaw: The two-week comparison between groups that share reviewers does too little to separate the paid half-day’s effect from differences in queue volume, PR complexity, and cross-group help.

claude.worst_flaw: A group-level paid half-day for hitting 80% on time is a high-stakes cliff reward for an audience already sceptical of gamification. It is tested only through a short, admittedly contaminated staggered comparison, with no plain-feedback-only arm to isolate what the reward adds. That leaves rushed rubber-stamp reviews as the main risk, and a 5-review weekly sample may be too small to catch them.

holistic.reason: Fixes the workflow first, ties a valued team-wide reward to a clear, audited, quality-guarded metric with a decision rule, which suits sceptical engineers, though a half-day off may not fully shift habits once the prize ends and the metric rules are complex to administer.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design has two rotations, randomised only by the order of their reward windows. That gives one effective comparison unit and contaminated within-team spillovers, so the reward's incremental value can't be separated from time trends or shared workflow fixes. The keep/stop thresholds also apply to the whole package, not to the reward itself.

codex.worst_flaw: With only one rotation per condition and both rotations expecting a reward, the pilot cannot reliably isolate the reward’s effect from differences between rotations, anticipation, or spillover.

holistic.reason: Thoughtful design that fixes root causes (rotation, protected time, routing), keeps the reward modest and team-based with private individual data, but it is elaborate for a 25-person team, leaves the 'useful review' judgment and sampling open to gaming and disputes, and lasting effect rests mainly on the routing that stays on after the prize ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The 80% retention rule can pass with one logged action per shift even if nearly all eligible moments go unlogged and observed compliance declines after rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: After the reward ends, the follow-up only tracks how widely the kiosk is used across shifts, not observed hand-hygiene compliance, and the design never shows the kiosk logging is worth the time nurses spend on it.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with audit-based rewards, workflow fixes, safety triggers and a sensible stagger, but ward-level pooled rewards risk diffuse motivation, the awareness of a meal plus thanks is modest, and durability depends on the workflow fixes rather than on any lasting incentive.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot support a kiosk rollout decision because the reward and exit rules measure clinical compliance while aggregate kiosk totals cannot establish what share of eligible moments nurses recorded correctly in the new system.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward is paid on monthly observer audits that staff know about and that sample few opportunities, so a Hawthorne-inflated or small-sample audit can trigger payouts. The design names this risk but sets no minimum sample size, never compares the audit against an independent or covert check, and gives the kiosk logging the hospital asked for no defined adoption or quality measure.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with sound audit-based measurement, usability fixes, safeguards against gaming and a staggered rollout, but a single shared meal at ward level is a modest, delayed incentive that nurses may barely notice, and the lasting effect depends mostly on the workflow fixes rather than on the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward depends only on observed audit compliance, yet nothing checks for Hawthorne or observer-recognition effects, and because a whole ward earns it, the pilot never asks whether the group reward creates peer pressure or makes nurses hide missed moments. Its correction and appeal process also rests on a single educator, with no versioned event history and no independent check against the kiosk.

codex.worst_flaw: The logging pilot is not launch-ready because counting shifts with at least one saved entry cannot establish what share of eligible hand-hygiene moments nurses record.

holistic.reason: The ward-level paid break rewarded on audited compliance, with kiosk entries carrying no reward value and a staggered rollout with clear end rules, is well designed and fundable. It is complex, though, and the ward-level reward is diffuse for individual nurses. Habits may fade once the break reward stops, so retention after three months is doubtful.

codex.worst_flaw: The pooled quality sample can pass even if a team earns lunch through poor-quality links, because the design sets no minimum sample or pass threshold for each team.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never reconciles the new knowledge-base reward with the existing CSAT bonus. Agents can lose CSAT pay when they flag gaps or take time to write articles, and a team lunch tied to a 40% threshold creates group pressure. Neither the incentive interaction nor the risk of pushing low-quality links to hit the team target has a test or safeguard.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with quality checks, CSAT guardrails, fair measurement and a sensible exit rule, though the team-lunch reward is modest and its salience is limited, so durability depends on the workflow fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout denominator includes tickets that cannot safely or usefully be documented, making the 40% target unfair across case mixes and creating pressure to attach unsuitable articles.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no appeal or dispute process and no versioned event history for credit corrections. Tickets that legitimately have no reusable article still count in each agent's 40% denominator, so agents with hard or novel case mixes are penalised and pushed toward linking irrelevant articles.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with pilot, staggered rollout, quality audits, and workflow left in place, but a one-credit-per-ticket 40% goal with modest 45-minute reward may feel low-stakes, and lasting change depends on the tool fixes rather than the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The retention decision compares quality-adjusted post-reward adoption with a baseline that lacks an equivalent usefulness audit, leaving the core improvement measure invalid.

claude.worst_flaw: The 30% target is a flat rate with no minimum ticket count and no adjustment for case mix, so agents with small books or queues where articles rarely apply are treated unevenly; the staggered team comparison also has few pairs, gives no sample size or uncertainty handling, and has no replayable record or independent shadow validation of credit.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with fair baseline, anti-gaming QA, CSAT guardrails and a staggered evaluation, but a one-hour prize for a 30% goal is modest, and the proposal's rigor and admin load (QA sampling, staggered cohorts) may outweigh agents' motivation and drive only a modest lasting habit.
